links.label: Figure 1.1. The start and selected goal both satisfy the whole-link clearance requirement. The dashed ring lies 5 mm outside the disc. The smallest link clearance is 49.9 mm at the start and 100.3 mm at the goal.

Figure 1.2. Linear interpolation of the joint angles carries link 2 through the disc. The curve shows the smaller link clearance at 43 sampled postures. It first falls below the 5 mm requirement at check 9; the halfway posture, check 21, has the deepest sampled penetration.

Figure 1.3. Arm postures A, B and C on the left correspond to the marked points on the right. The shaded configurations violate the 5 mm requirement. The direct connection crosses that region; a three-segment detour goes around it. The inset locates this enlarged view in the full bounded chart.

Figure 2.1. Two objectives with the same start, positive-elbow goal and final rest, with the obstacle removed. The left panel plots the Euclidean size of each joint-angle step. The right panel shows the common tip route and the different tip positions at knot indices 4, 10 and 16. Squares mark the velocity-cost motion and circles the acceleration-cost motion. Markers with the same number show both motions at the same normalized time.

Figure 2.2. A feature of order zero uses one configuration; first and second differences use two and three neighboring configurations. These local dependencies make most blocks of the trajectory Jacobian zero.

Figure 2.3. Default solver options return the same knots from both initial guesses. The red square marks knot 13, where link 2 misses the required clearance by 2.0 mm. The gray region contains postures that intersect the disc; the pale band contains postures that clear it by less than 5 mm.

Figure 2.4. Accurate reference. Workspace close-up of link 2 at knots 12 (blue) and 13 (green), and halfway between them (red). The gray circle is the physical disc and the dashed circle lies 5 mm outside it. The cross marks the intermediate posture’s nearest point, 1.84 mm inside the ring and still outside the disc.
Figure 3.1. A roadmap supplies several checked connections. Graph search selects the blue five-edge route. Matching labels identify its four intermediate postures in joint space and in the workspace.

Figure 3.2. Following parents extracts the highlighted start-to-goal route from the RRT. The workspace panel shows its arm postures; the joint-space panel also shows branches that are not part of the returned route.

Figure 3.3. Blue and green trees grow from opposite endpoints. Their parent chains form the purple route through the orange joining segment. The workspace panel shows postures along that returned route.

Figure 3.4. One RRT* insertion creates a cheaper route to the marked neighbor. Its descendants inherit the saving, including the goal. Orange marks the adopted connections. This illustration uses a 10° neighborhood and shows one insertion, not a complete RRT* run.

Figure 4.1. The sampled route supplies 21 initial configurations. Connecting successive knots can cut across an old corner. The new connection in the close-up misses the required clearance by 0.30 mm.

Figure 4.2. The direct and sampled initial guesses lead to the same optimized knots in this example. The overlapping markers show agreement between the two results; they do not establish global optimality or a speed advantage.

Figure 4.3. Optimization lowers the sampled acceleration cost but increases the largest scanned clearance deficit between knots. Neither cost reduction nor accurate knot constraints establish clearance along the connecting motion.

Figure C.1. Shortcutting reduces route length, but its passing coarse check misses a small buffer violation. The close-up shows the arm approaching the 5 mm boundary; the finer scan finds about 0.09 mm missing clearance.
